top_choice_rationale: P001 (B001, Helpman and Melitz) rewards one identifiable, mature discovery. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) showed that firms differ in productivity and select into exporting and foreign investment, so trade reallocates activity across firms and adds a channel to the gains from trade. The selection and sorting predictions have been tested in firm-level data across many countries for more than twenty years, and where the baseline failed in detail the literature extended it and kept the selection logic. The framework has also changed how macro, growth and productivity work treats reallocation. The credit rests on a small set of papers. The main risk is attribution: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions and are not credited, and Redding's quantitative-trade work is excluded. I judge this manageable if the citation is confined to selection and reallocation, makes no claim about welfare magnitudes (which depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions), and does not claim the exporter-premia facts or the whole firm-level trade programme. Whether the discovery is the model or the model plus the empirical programme is a judgement the record does not settle. Agreement among the eleven round-2 files is not independent evidence of merit, so this ranking rests on the content of the discovery, not on the count. Only P000 and P001 are on the slate. I rank P000 below P001 because the case for an award is strong, and B006 and B034 do not appear as proposals.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile for Helpman or Melitz. Disclosed but not adjudicated: I am Secretary of the Committee. Timo Boppart (co-opted member) and John Hassler (chair) are co-authors, and neither is a credited name on P001. My field of dynamic macro and heterogeneous-agent models is adjacent to the reallocation literature that the B001 framework fed, which may bias my view of its reach.
